outline.description: This chapter introduces the petitioners, their background in Colombia, the events leading to their departure for the United States, and the procedural history of their immigration proceedings from Notices to Appear through the BIA appeal and Tenth Circuit review.
subtopics: Petitioners' personal and professional background in Bogota, Colombia
Petitioners' political activities with the Colombian Liberal Party and 2022 presidential campaign
Jimenez's legal work and the property dispute involving Don Rafa, a narco-trafficking guerrilla leader
Escalation of threats and intimidation against the family
DHS Notices to Appear and removal proceedings before the Immigration Judge
IJ's denial of asylum, withholding of removal, and CAT claims; BIA affirmance
Scope of appeal before the Tenth Circuit (asylum and withholding only; CAT and due process claims not appealed)

outline.chapter_title: Legal Framework for Asylum and Withholding of Removal
outline.description: This chapter explains the statutory and regulatory framework governing asylum and withholding of removal claims, including the definition of a refugee, the burden of proof, and the elements an applicant must establish to qualify for relief.
subtopics: Jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. § 1252 and standard of review (substantial evidence)
Definition of 'refugee' under the INA (8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A))
Burden of proving refugee status by a preponderance of the evidence
The three elements of past persecution: harm rising to persecution, nexus to a protected ground, and government inability or unwillingness to protect
Presumption of well-founded fear of future persecution from past persecution
Relationship between asylum (lower standard) and withholding of removal (higher standard)
Role of the BIA decision versus the IJ's more complete explanation on appeal

outline.description: This chapter examines the Tenth Circuit's analysis of whether the harm Petitioners suffered—threats, emotional distress, and the assault of an employee—rose to the level of persecution under the INA, applying the cumulative effects test and relevant precedent.
subtopics: The INA's lack of a statutory definition of persecution and the Tenth Circuit's interpretive standard
Requirement that persecution entail suffering or harm that is offensive and more than mere restrictions or threats
Cumulative effects analysis: considering multiple incidents collectively
Why threats alone are insufficient to constitute persecution under Tenth Circuit precedent
Petitioners' concession that they suffered no physical harm and its significance
Insufficiency of emotional and psychological harm without physical harm
Comparison to prior Tenth Circuit cases involving more extreme harm that still failed the persecution threshold
Application of these principles to Petitioners' facts and the court's conclusion

outline.chapter_title: Nexus to a Statutorily Protected Ground
outline.description: This chapter analyzes whether Petitioners established that the harm they suffered was 'on account of' their political opinion, focusing on the 'at least one central reason' standard and the mixed-motive analysis.
subtopics: The nexus requirement: harm must be 'on account of' a protected ground
Petitioners' argument that they were targeted for their political opinion supporting a rival of Colombia's president
The 'at least one central reason' standard under 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(1)(B)(i)
Mixed-motive analysis: a persecutor may have multiple motives, but at least one protected ground must be a central reason
Petitioners' failure to brief particular social group arguments, limiting review to political opinion
The court's finding that Don Rafa's primary motive was personal—protecting his revenue and property—not Petitioners' political opinion
Evidence that escalated threats began only after the property dispute, not during prior political campaigning
The court's conclusion that political opinion was tangential and subordinate to the personal motive

outline.chapter_title: Government Protection, Safe Relocation, and Disposition
outline.description: This chapter covers the court's analysis of whether the Colombian government was unable or unwilling to protect Petitioners, whether internal relocation was feasible, and the final disposition denying the petition for review.
subtopics: The unable-or-unwilling analysis and the two key factors: government efforts to stop persecutors and government offers of protection
Importance of whether the applicant reported persecution to the government and gave the government an opportunity to respond
Petitioners' minimal efforts to seek government help and failure to report through available channels
Distinction between individual police apathy and systemic government failure
Evidence undermining Petitioners' argument: government had attempted searches and seizures at Don Rafa's property
Petitioners' failure to demonstrate that contacting the government would have been futile or dangerous
Safe internal relocation analysis under 8 C.F.R. § 1208.13(b)(1)(i)
Evidence supporting feasibility of relocation: family safety in Colombia, prior safe relocation to countryside, and persecutors' limited geographic threat
Court's rejection of Petitioners' counterarguments about economic burdens and government ties to persecutors
Final disposition: denial of asylum and consequent failure of withholding of removal under the higher standard
